title: Small Cells, Big Planet
question: Why do bacteria matter so much to life on Earth?
hook: Cells a few micrometres long recycle nutrients, and ancient ones were taken into other cells and never left.
idea: Bacteria live in nearly every habitat, recycle nutrients, and ancient ones became parts of eukaryotic cells such as mitochondria and chloroplasts.

beats.prompt: Researchers sample acidic hot springs and radioactive waste, expecting nothing could live there. What do they find?

choices.label: Nothing alive at all
choices.feedback: It seems too harsh for life, but bacteria are present in even such extreme environments.

choices.label: Only plants and animals
choices.feedback: Plants and animals are less likely in such places, while bacteria live there, as well as in soil and underwater.

beats.explain: Bacteria live in every possible habitat, including acidic hot springs and radioactive waste.

beats.prompt: Put these steps in the order they happened.
items: Single-celled ancestors of bacteria become the first forms of life
Proto-eukaryotic cells engulf alphaproteobacterial symbionts that become mitochondria
Eukaryotes that already hold mitochondria engulf cyanobacteria-like organisms
Chloroplasts form in algae and plants
beats.explain: Bacterial ancestors came first, mitochondria followed, and later engulfing of cyanobacteria-like organisms led to chloroplasts.

beats.prompt: Match each job to the bacterial process behind it.
beats.explain: Bacteria drive each of these, from food-making to mining to the nutrient cycle.

beats.prompt: This reasoning about bacteria has one wrong step. Which?
steps: The term bacteria traditionally included all prokaryotes.
In the 1990s prokaryotes were found to consist of two very different groups, Bacteria and Archaea.
Those two groups evolved from an ancient common ancestor.
So Bacteria and Archaea must be one and the same group after all.
beats.explain: They share an ancient ancestor but are very different groups, and they are called separate evolutionary domains.
